rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites avoid fighting and, if they join, refuse to risk wealth or life; they want the status of martyrs and warriors without bloodshed.
rows.anchor: They desired to become martyrs and ghāzīs without spilling a single drop of blood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their eyes dart about when danger comes because they fight for appearance rather than sacrifice; even slight danger exposes the pretence.
rows.anchor: Only that person can stare death in the face who has the intention to be martyred in the way of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb salaq means speaking in a sweet, flattering tone and describes the hypocrites’ sharp-tongued address.
rows.anchor: The word سلق means to talk in a sweet and flattering tone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once danger passes, they flatteringly claim that their own courage stopped the enemy, although danger had been close.
rows.anchor: as if it was their valour and courage which stopped the enemy from advancing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their tongues sharpen from greed for wealth as they seek the largest possible share of the spoils.
rows.anchor: their tongues would become sharp in greed for wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated term shuhh parallels the verse’s opening: it means stinginess there and greed here, two aspects of one character.
rows.anchor: Both these meanings are two aspects of the same personality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will not shed a drop of blood or spend a penny for Muslims, yet become accusatory in their greed for war spoils.
rows.anchor: they are not willing to spill even a single drop of blood nor spend a single penny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their talk has a biting edge: to secure spoils they blame, censure, and curse others, even accusing the Prophet of biased distribution.
rows.anchor: blame, censure and curse others to obtain these spoils.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They claim faith only with their tongues; God wastes their outwardly religious deeds, which earn no afterlife reward without faith.
rows.anchor: these people lay claim to faith merely through their tongues; they do not actually profess faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepts small or great deeds only when they follow His directives and are done purely to please Him; deeds done for others are rejected, even great pilgrimage or jihad.
rows.anchor: accepts every deed, whether small or big, which is done in accordance with His directives and purely to please Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human admiration of a deed cannot secure its afterlife reward: even the greatest deed has no divine weight without the right intention, and God needs no deed.
rows.anchor: The greatest of deeds has no weight in the eyes of God if it is not done to please Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can easily reject deeds done for others and direct their doers to seek reward from those they served.
rows.anchor: will ask its doers to demand its reward from those for whom they did it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although God is merciful, His honour and self-sufficiency mean He rejects deeds whose acceptance would violate His honour.
rows.anchor: He is also has a great sense of honour and is self-sufficient.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even after the enemy groups have been defeated and gone home, the hypocrites remain so terrified that they imagine the enemy is still present.
rows.anchor: the hearts of these Hypocrites are struck with such awe and terror

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They remain in Madīnah unwillingly and would rather live among Bedouins, asking from there what is happening to the Muslims if another attack threatens.
rows.anchor: they would desire to go and live with the Bedouins in their villages instead of remaining in Madīnah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if they stay with the Muslims, they would scarcely fight; their absence is preferable so their corrupting influence does not affect others.
rows.anchor: Even if they remain with them, they are not those who will participate in a battle.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger faced every danger at the front, so the cowards are shamed for failing to follow his example.
rows.anchor: present among them at the battle front was God’s Messenger and they observed through their very eyes how he faced all the dangers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not everyone who claims to follow the Messenger can emulate him; only those hoping for God and the Hereafter can endure this path and trial.
rows.anchor: Only those people can face the trial of this path who hope to meet God and await the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Steadfastness on the path of truth requires strong faith in God and the Hereafter, continually refreshed by remembrance of God.
rows.anchor: only those people are steadfast and resolute in the path of truth who have a strong faith in God and in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites lack faith in God and the Hereafter and remembrance of Him, explaining why fear remained even after the enemy was routed.
rows.anchor: the Hypocrites neither have faith in God and in the Hereafter nor keep God in their remembrance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites and jealous spread the claim that God’s and His Messenger’s promises were false; this verse gives the true believers’ contrary response.
rows.anchor: seeing the vast expanse of the enemy army they began to spread the propaganda among the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers recognize this ordeal as the test God and His messengers had foretold before eventual success.
rows.anchor: the same test of which they were already pre-informed by God and His messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi links the established practice of testing believers to Sūrah al-‘Ankabūt’s account of believers being tested.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah al-‘Ankabūt, this established practice is referred to by the words:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an says believers are tested so God can distinguish those truthful in faith from liars.
rows.anchor: Thus God will definitely make distinct those who are truthful in their claim to faith from those who are liars.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s and His Messenger’s promise proved true; those steadfast through this trial will also witness the promised conquest of Rome and Persia.
rows.anchor: will become the masters of the treasures of Rome and Persia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trial increased believers’ faith and obedience; trials distinguish the truthful from the weak, in keeping with God’s established practice.
rows.anchor: this test did not weaken them; in fact, it only augmented their faith and obedience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unqualified word rijāl magnifies the noun; “righteous people” or “commendable people” conveys its sense.
rows.anchor: serves to magnify the noun.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word nahb has a broad sense that includes determination, resoluteness, promises, and vows.
rows.anchor: Thus, determination, resoluteness, promises, vows are included in it.

rows.speaker: Imām al-Bukhārī
rows.claim: Imām al-Bukhārī explains nahb as a promise, which Islahi says fits the word and context.
rows.anchor: Imām al-Bukhārī 61 says that it means  دهع promise)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike hypocrites who had promised not to retreat but made excuses when battle came, some believers sacrificed their lives to fulfil their promise and others remain ready.
rows.anchor: when the time came, they began finding excuses to run away.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers who are still awaiting their sacrifice have not altered their commitment to God.
rows.anchor: they did not change the slightest the promise they made with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted verb is understood from context: God brought about the Battle of the Trench to distinguish the righteous from hypocrites, rewarding the former and possibly punishing or forgiving the latter.
rows.anchor: God stirred this battle of the ditch so that it can become a yardstick to judge the righteous from the Hypocrites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “if He wills” is omitted after the mention of accepting their repentance to avoid needless repetition; divine will follows wisdom and established practice.
rows.anchor: to do away with needless repetition. The will of God is subservient to His wisdom and established practice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse invites the hypocrites to repent: if they do, God may forgive them, and they should entrust themselves to Him rather than false supports.
rows.anchor: The words of this verse invite the Hypocrites to repent and tell them that there is still a chance for this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpreting forgiveness as available without repentance misunderstands God’s established practice; His will remains governed by wisdom and justice.
rows.anchor: have failed to understand the established practice of God regarding repentance.
